title: Will GUI-based game engines fall behind code-based ones in the age of AI coding?
author: Over_Value1408
selftext:
We’ve entered the era of AI-assisted coding. Vive coding with LLMs is becoming a part of daily development. Yet, in the game industry, this hasn’t been fully embraced—most AI-driven outputs are still limited to simple web-based mini games.

I think one major reason is that most game engines still rely heavily on GUI-based editors. But today’s dominant AI models are LLMs—*language* models. That means tools where you can develop 100% in code are naturally more compatible with AI coding workflows.

Of course, I’m aware that multimodal models are advancing quickly. LLMs can now interpret images, and it’s easy to imagine screen-recognizing AI agents becoming mainstream soon. Still, even then, I feel that from an efficiency standpoint, code-based engines will always be more advantageous when paired with AI.

And yes—I do believe that in the far future we’ll eventually reach the point where you can just *say* what you want, and an AI will build a perfect, fully functional game. But I’m not talking about that distant future here. I’m thinking more about the near term, where code-first approaches seem better aligned with the AI tools we already have.

What do you think—will GUI-first engines adapt, or will code-first engines gain the upper hand in the AI era?

comments.author: JaWoodyReddit
comments.body: No and anyone would be delusional to think so

replies.author: MrEktidd
replies.body:
Delusional is a wild word for believing AI will keep improving.

It very obviously will continue to get better and better.

You'd have to be delusional to see the progress of the last few years, and think that's where it stops. 

Come on.

replies.author: Rrrrry123
replies.body:
Has there been much improvement though? Type something into Google and the AI summary is most likely wrong in some regard. Generate an image or some writing and people will be able to tell you it's AI in no time.

Also, at some point, these companies are going to run out of good training data. What do you train an AI on when everything online is AI generated?

comments.author: Previous_Host_9990
comments.body:
This is exactly why I'm betting on a resurgance of web games. 

LLMs are amazing at building websites and backends to power them, totally in code. For graphics heavy games it might be infeasible at the moment. But for simpler games, and for devs wanting to lean into AI, I think web is a nice option.

replies.body: I just banged out a prototype in PhaserJS and feel this comment personally

comments.author: o_herman
comments.body:
We need screen-reading AIs to be able to automate GUI-based editors.

As for vibe coding, it's currently a hit-or-miss thing, but give it a few more months and years and quality will catch up. By then, you can probably build a complete full-featured game in one afternoon.

replies.author: doorknob123
replies.body: Tools like Bezi are moving in this direction. It’s a hard problem to solve though, automating GUI based editors requires the AI to understand so much of the possible actions in the editor as well as the scene. It’s not as simple as automating something purely text based, like code editors.

replies.author: o_herman
replies.body:
And screen reading is a whole different Pandora’s box. You’d need not just OCR-level interpretation, but a full semantic mapping of what’s in the framebuffer or compositing layer. That implies an API layer that can expose the GUI state in a structured way with widgets, hierarchy, properties - rather than raw pixels. 

Otherwise the AI has to reconstruct intent from screenshots, which is fragile and computationally heavy. Without standardized accessibility hooks or editor-specific APIs, automating GUIs will always lag behind text-based environments.

comments.author: ByEthanFox
comments.body:
>most AI-driven outputs are still limited to simple web-based mini games.

>I think one major reason is that most game engines still rely heavily on GUI-based editors

I think it's because *most* AI-embracing developers aren't doing it for the love of the game, but rather, the love of money. They're trying to use AI to make the next Flappy Bird, i.e. a small in scope game that they can put online, make a bunch of money off then retire.

These tools are of less interest to developers who want to make large-in-scope passion projects because in the case of those, the work, the process, they're part of the point.

And even if you're pro-AI dev, surely you can agree that *many* people getting into AI are doing it for this reason; it's either an idle curiosity or it's to try and get-rich-quick.

comments.author: MattDTO
comments.body: I think the future would be better workflows for vibe coding. Like you really need a human to tell the LLM what to do, otherwise it goes off the rails. So the human could have access to both a GUI and the code, same with the LLM. But the LLM could have MCP/Tools to do things in the GUI, so it doesn't need to screen read to figure out what to click on. And you need a human there to explain whether the game is fun, art looks good, etc. An agent can't figure out that your physics are too floaty, or the particle effect look terrible.
